canonical_topic: Two chemical forms of sulfur in coal
definition: Sulfur in coal exists in two distinct forms — pyrite (iron-bound) and organic sulfur (carbon-bound) — and each requires a different removal technique.
core_idea: Most coal sulfur is bound with iron as pyrite crystals ('fool's gold') physically scattered through the coal, while the remainder is chemically bonded to the coal's carbon as organic sulfur; because the two forms are held differently, pyrite can be mechanically separated before combustion but organic sulfur can only be addressed after combustion, via stack scrubbers.
key_points: Pyrite is the more common sulfur form, an iron-sulfur mineral distinct from the coal matrix
Organic sulfur is chemically bonded to the coal's carbon and cannot be physically separated
Pyrite is removable pre-combustion; organic sulfur removal requires post-combustion exhaust scrubbing
relationships: Organic sulfur removal → flue gas desulfurization
trading_implications: Sulfur form/content affects processing and compliance costs baked into delivered coal economics
caveats: Not all sulfur in coal can be removed the same way — the removal method depends on which chemical form is present
